title: Creating a 2D Top Down Game!
author: Dramatic_Post2968
selftext:
I am working on a kid’s game - **Building a hand-illustrated 2D exploration game — top-down or isometric?**  
I’m creating a 2D exploration game with a **hand-illustrated / graphic-artist style** rather than pixel art.  
Exploration and discovering new things is the core of the game, so I want every map to feel fresh, with mostly new assets and environments rather than repeatedly rearranging the same trees, rocks, props, etc.  
I’m currently leaning toward an **elevated top-down / 3/4 view**, but wondering if isometric or another perspective would work better.  
For this kind of game, what approach would you recommend? And would you build maps using modular illustrated assets, larger illustrated backgrounds, or a mix of both?

comments.author: Kashmakers
comments.body:
You want to create assets that you can re-use. Otherwise you're just letting AI generate every map and it's going to be inconsistent.

A top down view is fine for this style. Isometric works better if you have re-usable assets and intend to add decoration/building in the game, which makes it much easier to place objects.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
I personally would use special locations the way we used to have sticker figurines\\object in kids sticker books.  
  
Meaning, that there is a more or less uniform underlying map\\background, and "stickers\\points of interests" are created to fit that background.  
Then you can shuffle them around, because they are designed to blend and fit with predefined background.  
So that cave has a greenish\\grassy outline\\foundation, and then you can move it anywhere, without a need to redo background every time you don\`t like its initial location.

Modular for sure, because if you might want to reuse that asset, in let say, snowy map, and then you don\`t need to redraw things, but just cover them with snow etc. Or make them covered with a fog and look a bit different etc.

Obviously if you feel like creating tons of specific assets for specific situation and have time to manage that - go for it, but there is a good reason people are reusing assets - not always due to being lazy, but also to keep style and scale consistent.   
And to be able to apply creative changes to a manageable amount of objects.  
  
If you at some point decide that gazzilion of your house images need chimney added on them - you don\`t need to go through all of them, but just through 4-5 images.

replies.author: Dramatic_Post2968
replies.body:
I do have a base terrain stitched with a 8-10 illustrations, and then place png assets on top of them.   
But every map is going to be a different place.   
Map 1 will be forest, so we may need 20 such assets.   
Map 2 may be dessert, so we need 20 assets there.   
Map 3 might be city, so we need 20 assets there.

comments.author: Lavaflame666
comments.body: Unless you are working with modular assets or grids i would go for di/trimetric

replies.author: Dramatic_Post2968
replies.body: Thanks for the inputs- Can you explain a little bit more on this ?

replies.author: Lavaflame666
replies.body: An isometric artstyle means You are looking down at a 45 degreee angle with an orthographic camera. So all sides have equal measurements. Isometric means "equal measure". Since there is no perspective and all angles are the same, they can easily be made into modular parts.
